title: Not things, but judgments
hookLine: people are upset not by things but by their judgments about things (Enchiridion 5)
tomorrow: The horse is handsome, not you

cards: Two people are stuck in the same traffic jam, same lane, same minute. One is pounding the wheel, already rehearsing the apology to the boss. The other has turned up the radio and is singing badly.
Same cars, same delay, same red brake lights stretching to the bridge. So what, exactly, is upsetting the first driver? If it were the traffic, it would be upsetting both of them.
Section five of the handbook gives Epictetus' answer, and it fits in a single breath.

teach.h: NOT THE THINGS, BUT THE OPINIONS.
teach.b: In George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The Greek word for those opinions is dogmata, the plural of today's word.
Today, dogma sounds like rigid doctrine, something you're not allowed to question. In Epictetus' Greek it's humbler.

teach.h: DOGMA: WHAT SEEMS SO TO ME.
teach.b: It comes from a verb meaning to seem: a dogma is what seems so to you, the verdict you've passed before you notice you passed it. The traffic is a thing.
I'm going to be fired, this always happens to me: those are dogmata.

teach.h: SOCRATES, AND THE LADDER OF BLAME.
teach.b: His example: death isn't terrible, or it would have seemed so to Socrates, who faced his own calmly. The terrible part is the judgment that death is terrible.
You can disagree with him about death and still try the move on a parking ticket. Then he adds a ladder.
An untrained person blames others when things go badly; someone starting out blames themself; someone trained blames neither. The sentence has a long echo.

teach.h: FROM STERNE TO THE THERAPY ROOM.
teach.b: The novelist Laurence Sterne put it, in Greek, at the front of Tristram Shandy.
In the twentieth century the psychologist Albert Ellis named Epictetus as an influence on his therapy, which taught people to catch the belief that sits between an event and the feeling.
Here is the honest limit. Epictetus isn't saying pain is imaginary or that nothing out there is wrong. He's saying the part that churns inside is built partly from our own verdicts.
And a verdict can be looked at again.

how: People who practice Stoicism often separate what happened from the judgment they've added to it, sometimes writing the two side by side.

o: a rigid doctrine nobody is allowed to question
a fact about the world that everyone can see
a judgment, what seems so to you about a thing

games.q: not things, but judgments — tap the pairs.

s: in Epictetus' Greek, dogma means a rigid doctrine you can't question
it means a judgment or opinion, what seems so to you.
Laurence Sterne put this line in Greek at the front of Tristram Shandy
the handbook's fifth section opens the novel.
he says our judgments about things are what disturb us, not that nothing happens.

games.q: your project went badly. on Epictetus' ladder, what does someone fully trained do?
games.why: the untrained blame others, beginners blame themselves, the trained blame neither and look at their judgments.

practice: Bring back one small thing that upset you this week, a text, a delay, a look, and first describe only what a camera would see: he replied with one word; the train came twelve minutes late.
Then find the judgment underneath, he's annoyed with me, my whole day is ruined, and add plainly: it's my view. Don't argue with it yet; just see that it's a view, sitting there.

wordCard.voice: Dogma. In Epictetus' Greek, not rigid doctrine but a judgment, what seems so to you. It's our dogmata, he says, that disturb us. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 5: a judgment, an opinion; from a verb meaning to seem.

carryVoice: Your line: it's my view. What happened is one thing; what I say about it is another. Until tomorrow.
